div.div:
In a modern multi-socket server (like an r6i.8xlarge), the CPUs are split into NUMA Nodes.
Each "node" has its own group of CPU cores and its own dedicated bank of local RAM.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(#ffffff, var(--ge-dark-color, #121212)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 218px; height: 1px; padding-top: 30px; margin-left: 811px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div:
Local Access:
A CPU core accessing RAM attached to its own socket is incredibly fast (low latency).

rect.style: fill: light-dark(#ffffff, var(--ge-dark-color, #121212)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 398px; height: 1px; padding-top: 170px; margin-left: 811px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div:
Remote Access:
If a CPU core needs data that is sitting in RAM attached to a different socket, it must travel across a "bridge" (like Intel's UPI or AMD's Infinity Fabric). This adds significant latency and reduces total bandwidth.

path.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 1px; height: 1px; padding-top: 100px; margin-left: 1272px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: nowrap;

div.div:
Without "Awareness," Kubernetes treats all RAM and CPUs as one big pool.
If a database pod is scheduled such that its vCPUs are on Socket 0 but its Data is in RAM on Socket 1, every single query faces a "tax" of remote memory latency.
Context Switching: The Linux kernel frequently moves your database process from one core to another to balance the load.Cache Thrashing:
When the process moves to a core on a different socket, it loses its L1/L2/L3 cache data, forcing it to fetch everything from RAM again.
On a large instance like an r6i.8xlarge (32 vCPUs), this "shuffling" can degrade your performance by 15–20%.
